stories.topic: The 1991 Reforms Were Twenty Years in the Making
stories.summary: Amit used to believe the 1991 reforms happened only because the balance of payments crisis left India no choice. Through his conversations on The Seen and the Unseen and Everything is Everything, he learned the story began much earlier. From the late 1960s Manmohan Singh was quietly building a community. He asked Vijay Kelkar to return to India in the early 1970s and Montek to return in the late 1970s. From then on, people inside and outside government worked out reform ideas, picked their battles, and avoided fights that could cost them their place. In 1990 Montek wrote the famous 'M document', which held much of what was done a year later. Ajay compared this to a relay race: we only watch the last runner cross the line, but the baton passed through many earlier hands.
stories.insight: A crisis looks like the cause of reform, but it only opened a window. The reform itself came from decades of patient, mostly invisible work by people who made sure the ideas were ready.
stories.quote: So when the ninety one crisis happened, everything was in place.

stories.topic: Two Failed Harvests and the Green Revolution
stories.summary: In the 1950s and 60s India's population grew fast while the food system stayed broken, even though many people knew what needed fixing. Then the kharif crops of 1965 and 1966 failed back to back, and India came close to mass starvation. The United States bailed India out through the PL 480 program, which gave concessional aid in the form of food grain. That humiliation concentrated minds. Indira Gandhi and C. Subramaniam pushed high-yielding varieties, fertilisers and irrigation, and the result was the Green Revolution.
stories.insight: This is the best case for crisis-driven reform, and Ajay offers it as the steelman. It shows a crisis can break a long deadlock when everyone already knew what the fixes were.
stories.quote: So India was reduced to taking development assistance in the form of food. And that's a pretty terrible place to be.

stories.topic: The Insider Who Couldn't See the House Was on Fire
stories.summary: Ajay remembers a well-known Indian economics bureaucrat who had been very good to him personally and who was part of the fiscal mess and balance of payments collapse of the late 1980s. In the run-up to 1991, this man stubbornly could not see that the system was broken. He was protecting his legacy and defending his own past decisions.
stories.insight: The people running a system when it breaks are the people least able to diagnose it. Fresh thinking in a crisis has to come from outside the establishment, so gathering establishment figures together in a crisis produces more of the same.
stories.quote: So the people who are inside the pressure cooker in a time of crisis are least able to understand that there's a problem.

stories.topic: How the Nirbhaya Moment Was Wasted
stories.summary: The horrific 2012 Nirbhaya rape case in Delhi brought the problem and the politics together. Ajay says Manmohan Singh and Montek wanted to use the moment to reform the criminal justice system. The policy groundwork did not exist. Nobody had spent twenty years building people, documents, books, seminars and an interconnected picture of how the system's parts fit together. The crisis produced only some activist-style lawmaking that didn't move the needle.
stories.insight: Public outrage and political will are not enough. If the ideas have not been developed in peacetime, the window closes with nothing to show for it.
stories.quote: a crisis is a terrible thing to waste, and the Nirbhaya crisis was wasted.

stories.topic: GST: Thirteen Years From Report to Reality
stories.summary: Vijay Kelkar, Arvind Modi and Ajay wrote the first fully worked-out proposal for a GST in 2003. The first real move towards a complete GST came in 2016, thirteen years later. Ajay thinks that is perfectly normal. Serious ideas need knowledge, philosophy, papers, books and endless debate before a country is ready for them.
stories.insight: Be suspicious of a 'we want action by the day after tomorrow' mindset. It produces trivial changes. Deep reform runs on a timescale of decades.
stories.quote: it takes five hundred seminars and conferences to argue about the GST. Then the country is spiritually ready to get to a GST.

stories.summary: Ajay treats the 1975 Emergency, which followed the Justice Sinha ruling, as the end point of a longer slide. The 1971 war created a huge fiscal problem. By 1974 inflation hit 16%, the highest in India's history. Society came apart: the JP Narayan movement, buses being burned, things falling apart. In that atmosphere Indira Gandhi suspended the rule of law.
stories.insight: This is the Indian version of Carl Schmitt's 'true ruler', someone who uses a crisis as cover to suspend the rule of law. The lesson is to fear crises in a country whose checks and balances are already weak.
stories.quote: Indira Gandhi was a true ruler. Who suspended rule of law in that time of crisis. Like what a catastrophe.

stories.topic: The Authoritarian Wish List That Waited for 9/11
stories.summary: A hawkish part of the US national security establishment had long been developing authoritarian tools: the Patriot Act, countering the financing of terror, anti-money laundering rules, and FATF, which in India shows up as the PMLA and the Enforcement Directorate. In normal times, principled lawmakers would have debated these and blocked them. After 9/11 they all passed within weeks. Ajay considers almost every piece a bad idea, and argues that tracing money flows has never disrupted a terrorist plot. What it did build was mass surveillance of finance.
stories.insight: This is the 1991 story with the sign flipped. Bad ideas can also be waiting in the policy pipeline, and a crisis lets them through just as easily as good ones.
stories.quote: And then came the 9/11 attacks and like whoosh, within weeks all this stuff got through.

stories.topic: Jim Comey's Dash to the Hospital
stories.summary: Ajay retells a story Jim Comey tells about a mass surveillance program. Comey, at the top of the US national security establishment, urgently rushed by car to a hospital to brief a desperately ill official before something bad was done about that program. Ajay contrasts this with weak democracies, where most people would just bow their heads and go along.
stories.insight: Checks and balances are not only written rules. They depend on individuals who will physically race across a city to defend the rule of law. That is why crises do less damage in mature democracies than in fledgling ones.
stories.quote: You need those people, you need those amazing people who will stand up and fight for the rule of law, but you need those checks and balances.

stories.topic: An Eight-Year-Old Versus Indira Gandhi on Inflation
stories.summary: In 1974 young Ajay watched Indira Gandhi blame the high inflation on hoarders and speculators. He was eight that year, and he already knew prices are set by supply and demand, not by villains. He was genuinely baffled that someone raised on 'all those beautiful letters', Glimpses of World History, could be so clueless. As an adult he understood it was not cluelessness. It was populism: making the elites the enemy so no one blames monetary policy, and building that into the Garibi Hatao ideology and attacks on things like privy purses.
stories.insight: When governments mismanage the economy, they look for a villain. Blaming hoarders shifts attention from bad policy to an 'other'.
stories.quote: When I grew up, I understood this is populism. You want to stoke hatred against the elites.

stories.summary: After demonetisation, with no prior planning, the RBI issued 74 regulations in 50 days, working things out on the fly and making a bad situation worse. During COVID the Ministry of Health issued 1,324 press releases. Ajay says this is what Lant Pritchett calls premature load bearing: an institution given more than it can carry collapses into organisational rout. He also cites the 2013 taper tantrum, set off by Ben Bernanke's remarks to a journalist. There, he says, the RBI and the Ministry of Finance misread the situation and turned a medium problem into a much bigger one.
stories.insight: A crisis does not need a villain to go wrong. A weak state reacting incoherently in a panic can do great damage by itself.
stories.quote: the Ministry of Health released 1,324 press releases at the time of COVID. Okay, now like what sense does that make?

stories.topic: Amit's Two Attempts to Move the Overton Window
stories.summary: Amit has tried to widen two Overton windows. The first is freedom. He calls himself a tariff absolutist (all tariffs should be zero) and a free speech absolutist, and says these are sincere beliefs, not tactics. This is a long game whose result is unknown. The second is podcast length, where he says he has won. When he started The Seen and the Unseen, people thought an hour was too long. After his ten-hour, twelve-hour and several eight-hour episodes, an hour no longer counts as a deep dive, and others in India now do three- and four-hour shows.
stories.insight: A position at the extreme makes moderate versions of the same idea sound reasonable. Amit's own career shows the window can move.
stories.quote: By taking the absolute position, you make other positions that are not so absolute sound relatively reasonable.

stories.topic: A Heart Scare, Diabetes, and the Lesson for Nations
stories.summary: Amit applies the argument to himself. A heart scare earlier this year (he got a stent) and, earlier, a diabetes diagnosis both pushed him into lifestyle 'reforms', and he reversed the diabetes through diet. But he could have died, and he knew all along what a healthy life looked like. He lacked the discipline to exercise, do resistance training, avoid sugar and sleep well. If he had, neither crisis would have happened. Likewise, if India had done the right things in the 1980s, there would have been no 1991 crisis. He then notes where the metaphor breaks: an individual can respond to a crisis far more coherently than a state, which is full of conflicting incentives and stakeholders. Ajay agreed with both halves of the point.
stories.insight: Celebrating a crisis that forced reform skips the real question, which is why the crisis was allowed to happen. Do the dull disciplined work in good times, and expect states to be much worse than individuals at improvising in an emergency.
stories.quote: It is in peace times that you win the next war by making sure the next war doesn't happen.

core_ideas.concept: Crises Are Dangerous, Not Golden Opportunities
core_ideas.explanation: Many Indians believe sweeping reform only happens in a crisis because 1991 worked that way. Amit says this confuses correlation with causation and suffers from selection bias, because it looks at one crisis that ended well and ignores the many that ended badly. Ajay's view is that the default reaction to a crisis should be fear, especially in a young democracy with weak checks and balances.
core_ideas.quote: I actually want to say this upside down that crises are truly dangerous times.

core_ideas.concept: Why Crises Seem to Work, and Why the Overton Window Cuts Both Ways
core_ideas.explanation: Here is the case for crises. Prospect theory says people treat the status quo as their reference point and, because of loss aversion, avoid rocking the boat. Special interests lock policy in place. When it seems the world is going to hell anyway, people become open to new ideas. Ajay frames this using the Overton window, the range of ideas acceptable in public discussion. A crisis widens it, which can make good ideas that were heresy become doable. It also normalises terrible ideas, and in poor countries that is more dangerous than in mature democracies.
core_ideas.quote: Well, many terrible ideas are also normalized when you have a crisis and the Overton window is widened. So you shouldn't be sure about which way this goes.

core_ideas.concept: The Real Problems Are Upstream of Policymakers
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay argues that helping a policymaker carry out what they already want, as consulting firms do, is not what matters. If you implemented everything a thousand good Indian policymakers want today, he doubts India would improve much. What matters is changing ideas and imagination, and building a group of independent thinkers who work on political economy and philosophy, not consulting. Without them a crisis brings no new ideas, only the same establishment voices.
core_ideas.quote: The problems are upstream. You need to change the ideas, you need to change the imagination, you need to build a cadre of people who are upstream of the policymakers

core_ideas.explanation: John Kingdon says change happens when three streams come together: a recognised problem, ready policy ideas, and favourable politics. In 1991 all three lined up. In the Nirbhaya case the problem and the politics lined up, but the policy ideas did not exist, so nothing came of it. A crisis can only bring the first and third. The second has to be built in advance.
core_ideas.quote: There is a problem stream, there's a policy stream, and there is a politics stream. All the three have to come together to get a meaningful process of change.

core_ideas.explanation: Shouting in the streets or on social media has its place, but real systems have many moving parts. You need people who have modelled the whole system in their heads. They know that changing one part forces changes elsewhere, which side effects to expect, and what order to do things in. Social media has produced many more activists, but not more of these people.
core_ideas.quote: If you don't have all that wonkery, then all the activism of the world is pointless.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay describes Carl Schmitt as a philosopher who helped give rise to the Nazis and to authoritarian thinking. Schmitt held that the true ruler is the one who can suspend the rule of law in a crisis. Ajay says this is exactly what to be afraid of. Examples: Indira Gandhi's Emergency after the 1974 inflation crisis, and Hitler using the Reichstag fire to suspend Weimar Germany's constitution. A crisis weakens the usual checks on power, and opportunists take advantage.
core_ideas.quote: He has a line which runs something like the true ruler is one who is able to suspend rule of law in a crisis.

core_ideas.concept: Inventing an 'Other' to Exploit or Create a Crisis
core_ideas.explanation: Amit adds another idea from Schmitt: politics requires an 'other'. In a crisis, the easy political move is to name an enemy, such as another community or 'the elites', present things as black and white, and play the victim even from a position of strength. Authoritarians use crises to gain power, and they also use this rhetoric to manufacture crises that justify taking more. Indira Gandhi blaming hoarders and speculators for inflation is Ajay's example.
core_ideas.quote: they will often use such rhetoric to create a crisis which they can then take advantage of to justify having more power.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay ties political disasters to monetary mistakes. Weimar Germany's hyperinflation came before Hitler, and India's 16% inflation in 1974 came before the Emergency. Hyperinflation destroys polite society and the basis of ordinary lives. Ajay says monetary economists deserve credit for the good since inflation targeting and blame for disasters like these. Amit adds that the blame also belongs to leaders who overrule monetary economists.
core_ideas.quote: Inflation tears the society apart. Just everything goes wrong and people get unhinged.

core_ideas.concept: Three Ways a Crisis Goes Wrong
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's summary. First, if no ideas were prepared, the crisis is simply wasted. Second, in a fragile state, malice: would-be autocrats suspend the rule of law, with Hitler as the extreme case. Third, in a state with low capability, incompetence: officials react with a flood of uncoordinated measures, as with demonetisation, COVID and the 2013 taper tantrum. Amit's use of Hanlon's razor ('never attribute to malice what can be adequately explained by stupidity') introduced the third path.
core_ideas.quote: Government is the power of giants given to pygmies who are trying to respond on a day to day basis on a crisis.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay uses Lant Pritchett's term. When a weak institution is suddenly given a heavy load, it does not rise to it. It collapses into organisational rout. The result is incoherence: practical people meeting each problem with a quick fix, with no shared strategy, so their actions work against each other. Coherence comes from thinking, which means understanding the world first and then applying one strategy to many problems.
core_ideas.quote: Coherence is an intellectual's word. It is a philosopher's word. It is about understanding the world and finding a common strategy that is then applied to disparate problems.

core_ideas.explanation: Karl Popper distinguished utopian social engineering, meaning grand plans such as collectivising every farm in the USSR, which usually end badly, from incremental engineering. Ajay compares two histories. The French Revolution tore society down and set France back for many years. Britain moved from monarchy to liberal democracy step by step, through gradual growth in Parliament's power, with Cromwell's execution of Charles I as the only dramatic moment, and became the most successful country in the world. Indian equity market reform from 1992 to 2007 is a local example of steady, data-driven progress.
core_ideas.quote: So we should be very mistrustful of grand schemes.

core_ideas.concept: Liberal in Ends, Conservative in Means
core_ideas.explanation: The hosts call themselves conservative in Edmund Burke's sense. That does not mean opposing change. It means being humble about how complex the world is. Every change has unintended consequences and knock-on effects nobody controls, so move one step at a time. If you move too fast, you break things without understanding what happened.
core_ideas.quote: I think both of us are liberal in our ends, conservative in our means.

core_ideas.concept: Fix the Roof While the Sun Is Shining
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's prescription for reformers: don't wait for a crisis and don't try to engineer one. Make progress every day in calm times by building people, ideas and communities one brick at a time. He asks for humility twice. Once because none of us understands the world well enough for grand plans, and again because we must admit when the evidence shows a step failed, then change course. A great country makes progress without needing a crisis.
core_ideas.quote: So fix the roof while the sun is shining, build the community, build the people, chip away, be a bricklayer.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Ajay asks who was key on the IMF side of the 1991 program. Amit answers Urjit Patel ('See, my GK is in place') and then mentions A.N. Varma, 'not related to me', who was also critical: 'So you get good things done with Varmas in the mix.'
On their weak YouTube numbers, Amit says: 'Do the right thing, don't worry about the fruits of your action. The Bhagavad Gita meets Spike Lee.'

Amit says Ajay wrote 'Chaos is a ladder' in In Service of the Republic on his own, only to find out later it is also in Game of Thrones. Amit voices Ajay's disappointment: 'it's such a great line I came up with it, but you know, if shit happens, man.'

Amit checks that Ajay's eighth birthday was 7 August 1974, the year of record inflation. Ajay: 'So I was like fully in the know by that time. Like supply and demand was something, you know, that every child knew. So why was Indira Gandhi so clueless?'
Playing on the letters collected as Glimpses of World History, Amit suggests a title for Ajay's next book: 'Glimpses of Good Economics.' Ajay agrees and promises to write letters of his own.
Amit introduces Hanlon's razor: 'Ajay, I love your beard, but I want to give to you a razor.'

Rain stops the outdoor recording. Ajay vows to carry on 'without an organisational rout', a callback to Lant Pritchett. Indoors, Amit says 'as our good friend Obelix would say, the sky fell on our heads.' He mentions his comfort bear Freddy, named after Bastiat and Hayek, is relieved Ajay 'did not throw a tantrum', and uses that to segue into the 2013 taper tantrum.

While reading the Weber quote, Ajay changes a 'he' to 'she' by habit. Amit points out that both hosts use the feminine pronoun by default, and says of Weber's time: 'That is the age where men were men.'
'A crisis is a terrible thing to waste' is attributed to Rahm Emanuel, Barack Obama's chief of staff. Ajay notes it plays on 'the mind is a terrible thing to waste.'

Ajay invokes 'the beautiful poem The Center Does Not Hold' for Weimar Germany, where communists and extremists crushed the centre. He sees 'more than a passing resemblance' in today's world, with 'crazy on both sides'.
The Reichstag fire, which Hitler used to monopolise power and suspend the constitution, is Ajay's prime example of a crisis seized by a 'true ruler'.
PL 480, the US program that sent India concessional food grain after the failed harvests of 1965–66.

Max Weber, read at the close: 'Politics is a strong and slow boring of hard boards. It takes both passion and perspective… even those who are neither leaders nor heroes must arm themselves with that steadfastness of heart which can brave even the crumbling of all hopes.'
